warmup.q: A Spark 3 job turns the text of each amount into a whole number, with CAST(amount_text AS INT). One line of the file says 12,50. The team upgrades to Spark 4.1 and keeps the default settings. What happens on that line?
options: It becomes NULL, SQL's blank, as before
It becomes 1250, because Spark 4 understands decimal commas
The job stops with an error named CAST_INVALID_INPUT
It becomes 12, the part before the comma
warmup.why: Spark 4.0 turned on ANSI mode by default, so a value that can't be turned into a number raises an error instead of becoming NULL. The NULL was Spark 3's behaviour, and it quietly dropped the line out of every sum, like the spreadsheet in the opening. try_cast gives the NULL back on purpose when that's what you want. Spark doesn't guess at number formats when it converts text.

sections.h: Spark Connect: your program sends a plan, a Spark server runs it
sections.html:
Every Spark program in the last three lessons started with a line like SparkSession.builder().master("local[2]"). That line starts the whole of Spark inside your own program. It starts the driver, the part that plans the work and hands out tasks. It starts the catalog (Spark's list of tables and their columns) and the optimizer, and on a laptop the executors that do the work, too. Your program runs on the JVM, the Java virtual machine that runs Java and Kotlin code. For a batch job, a program that starts, does one big piece of work and stops, that's fine.

Now picture the payments company's app for shop owners. It runs all day: an owner opens a page, and the app asks Spark for that shop's totals. A program like that, which runs all the time and answers requests, is called a service. Putting all of Spark inside a service causes three problems.

The first is the classpath, the list of jar files (bundles of compiled Java code) that a JVM program loads. Spark 4.1 brings hundreds: the demo's Spark JVM has 212 jars and folders on its classpath. Among them are popular libraries for networking, JSON and more (Netty, Jackson, Guava) and the client code for Hadoop, lesson 3's big-data system. Each must agree with the versions the service already uses. The second is memory. The driver's plans, its copies of broadcast tables (small tables it sends to every task) and the results it collects all live in the service's heap. That's the memory where a JVM keeps its objects. One collect() too many (a call that pulls a whole result into memory) takes the service's pages down with it. The third is upgrades: the Spark version is baked into the service, so upgrading Spark means shipping a new service.

Version 1: don't put Spark inside; hand jobs to it. Package the job as a jar and give it to spark-submit, Spark's command for starting a job on a cluster, a group of computers that work together. The service and Spark are apart now, but the service can't ask a question and get rows back.

Version 2: a client and a server, like ordering at a restaurant. You don't need a kitchen at home. You write down your order, hand it over, and the kitchen cooks. That's Spark Connect. The server is an ordinary Spark driver with the Connect plugin, waiting for calls on port 15002 by default. (A port is a number that tells a computer which program a network message is for.) The calls use gRPC, a way for one program to call another over the network, and the messages are encoded with protobuf, Google's compact binary format for structured data. The client is a small library that offers the same DataFrame calls (a DataFrame is Spark's table with named columns).

Building a DataFrame in the client builds a tree of plan steps and nothing more: no names are checked and nothing is sent. An action, a call such as collectAsList() that needs an answer, encodes the whole tree as one protobuf message and sends it, like handing over the whole order at once. The server checks the names against its catalog, optimizes the plan (everything from the last lesson happens on the server) and runs it on its executors. It streams the result back as Apache Arrow record batches. Arrow is a column-by-column format that both sides can read without converting. Spark 3.4 introduced Connect, and Spark 4.0 says its Java client covers the full API, the whole set of calls. The stepper below follows one query through it.

In the Try it, the client JVM has 57 jars and folders on its classpath and no Spark driver. The report travels as 1,661 bytes of protobuf, most of them notes on where in the code each call was made, for error messages. A misspelled column fails only at the action, when the server first sees the plan. A kitchen, too, notices a dish that isn't on the menu only when the order arrives. In classic Spark it would have failed on the line that built the DataFrame.

What can't cross is anything that lives only inside a driver. The client has no SparkContext (the driver's own handle on the cluster) and no RDDs (Spark's older API, from The Spark execution model). Both calls fail with UNSUPPORTED_CONNECT_FEATURE. Lambdas, functions written inline such as x -> x * 100, are the tricky case. A plan can say "call this function", but the function's compiled code lives in your client's classes, which the server doesn't have. It's a family recipe: the kitchen can't cook it until you send the card. Upload the classes first, a folder with registerClassFinder or a jar with addArtifact, and the same lambda runs.

The restaurant picture breaks at the reply: a kitchen sends one dish, while Spark streams the rows back in batches as they're ready. Connect changes where Spark runs. Next, a change in what Spark does with a value it can't read.

frames.say: What stays on the server can't be used from the client: sparkContext() and rdd() throw UNSUPPORTED_CONNECT_FEATURE. A lambda is code the server doesn't have. It runs only after the client uploads its class files with registerClassFinder, or a jar with addArtifact.

try.title: Run a client in one JVM and Spark in another
steps: From the labs folder, run ConnectDemo. It starts a Spark driver with the Connect plugin at 127.0.0.1:15002 (127.0.0.1 is a computer's address for itself). Then it starts SettlementClient as a second JVM whose classpath holds only the Connect client. Read the client's code too; it's the file shown.
Before you read the output: when the client builds the DataFrame with the misspelled column stauts, does anything fail?
Find where the explain() text was worked out, and count the jobs the server ran for the client.

code.title: SettlementClient.java (the client JVM; ConnectDemo.kt starts the server)
code.html: package sfz.batch.l09.client; import static org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col; import static org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.MapFunction; import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset; import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders; import org.apache.spark.sql.Row; import org.apache.spark.sql.connect.SparkSession; import org.apache.spark.sql.connect.client.REPLClassDirMonitor; /** * A Spark Connect client: no driver, no executors, no SparkContext in this JVM. It builds a * DataFrame, which is only a plan, and sends the plan to the server over gRPC. * * Arguments: the server URL (sc://host:port), the payments folder on the server's disk, and this * program's own classes folder (for the lambda at the end). */ public class SettlementClient { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String url = args[0]; String payments = args[1]; String classesDir = args[2]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder().remote(url).getOrCreate(); System.out.printf("client: %s, connected in %d ms, server runs Spark %s%n", spark.getClass().getSimpleName(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, spark.version()); System.out.printf("client: %d jars and folders on this JVM's classpath%n", System.getProperty("java.class.path").split(java.io.File.pathSeparator).length); // building the DataFrame runs nothing and contacts nobody: it is a tree of plan nodes Dataset<Row> report = spark.read().parquet(payments) .where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")) .groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total_cents")) .orderBy(col("total_cents").desc()) .limit(3); // the message that will cross the wire: an unresolved plan as protobuf. plan() is // package-private in Scala, so the client reaches it by reflection Object plan = report.getClass().getMethod("plan").invoke(report); byte[] bytes = (byte[]) plan.getClass().getMethod("toByteArray").invoke(plan); System.out.printf("client: the plan is a %s of %,d bytes. Without call-site details it reads:%n", plan.getClass().getSimpleName(), bytes.length); for (String line : withoutCommonBlocks(plan.toString())) System.out.println(" " + line); // the action: the server resolves, optimizes and runs the plan, and streams Arrow batches back System.out.println("client: top merchants " + report.collectAsList()); System.out.println("client: explain(), computed by the server:"); report.explain(); // the client checks nothing while you build: a misspelled column only fails when the server sees the plan Dataset<Row> typo = spark.read().parquet(payments).where(col("stauts").equalTo("CAPTURED")); System.out.println("client: built a DataFrame with a misspelled column, no error yet"); try { typo.count(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("client: count() -> " + firstLine(e)); } // what a thin client cannot do: there is no SparkContext and there are no RDDs on this side try { spark.sparkContext(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("client: sparkContext() -> " + firstLine(e)); } try { report.rdd(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("client: rdd() -> " + firstLine(e)); } // a typed lambda is bytecode the server doesn't have MapFunction<Long, Long> times100 = x -> x * 100; try { spark.range(3).map(times100, Encoders.LONG()).collectAsList(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("client: map(lambda) -> " + firstLine(e)); } // upload this program's class files, and the same lambda runs on the server spark.registerClassFinder(new REPLClassDirMonitor(Path.of(classesDir).toAbsolutePath().toString())); System.out.println("client: map(lambda) after registerClassFinder -> " + spark.range(3).map(times100, Encoders.LONG()).collectAsList()); System.exit(0); } /** The protobuf text without its `common { ... }` blocks, which carry plan ids and call sites. */ static List<String> withoutCommonBlocks(String text) { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); int skipping = 0; for (String line : text.split("\n")) { String t = line.trim(); if (skipping > 0) { if (t.endsWith("{")) skipping++; if (t.equals("}")) skipping--; continue; } if (t.equals("common {")) { skipping = 1; continue; } out.add(line); } return out; } static String firstLine(Throwable e) { String m = e.getMessage() == null ? "" : e.getMessage(); String first = m.split("\n")[0]; return e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + (first.length() > 160 ? first.substring(0, 160) + "..." : first); } }

(Paths shortened.) The plan the client printed is the query nested inside out: limit holds sort, which holds aggregate, which holds filter, which holds read. Every name in it is still an unresolved_attribute. The client never checked status against anything, which is why the misspelled stauts only failed when count() sent it. The explain() text, with its pushed filters and Exchange, came from the server's Catalyst. The two UNSUPPORTED_CONNECT_FEATURE errors are the things a thin client doesn't have. The lambda failed until the client uploaded its own class files; after registerClassFinder, the server loaded the class and ran it. All the work, 5 jobs and 7 tasks, ran in the server's JVM. Connecting took seconds here because the client JVM loads a 25 MB jar on a busy machine; on an idle laptop it's faster.

aside.title: Which Spark version should a project use?
aside.html: Not automatically the newest. Spark now ships a feature release every quarter: 4.0 in May 2025, 4.1 in December 2025, 4.2 in July 2026 and 4.3 on 30 October 2026, the first on the quarterly schedule. A job also needs the library for its table format, the code that keeps track of which files make up a table, and those libraries ship one build per Spark version. Iceberg 1.12 (September 2026) has builds for Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 only, and Delta Lake 4.4.1 supports 4.0.1, 4.1 and 4.2, so 4.1 is the newest version both support (lesson 11 opens Iceberg up). This track's labs therefore pin Spark 4.1.4 on JDK 21, the Java development kit: Spark 4.1 runs on Java 17 and 21, and Java 25 support arrived in 4.2. Everything in this lesson works on 4.1, and the few things that need 4.2 or 4.3 say so.

sections.h: ANSI mode: Spark 4 stops on bad data instead of leaving a blank
sections.html:
Back to the opening's spreadsheet, now as a file. Each night, the payments company gets a file from a card company that lists what each shop is owed. (The lab calls it a settlement file.) One line's amount is 12,50, because someone's spreadsheet used a decimal comma. The job turns the text into a number. What should happen?

Spark 3, by default, returned NULL, SQL's marker for "no value". CAST('12,50' AS INT), which converts text to a whole number, gave NULL. The line's amount dropped out of every sum, and the job finished as if all was well. Arithmetic behaved like Java's. An INT, a whole number of 32 bits that tops out at about 2.1 billion, wrapped around to a large negative number when it grew too big. And a division by zero gave NULL. Each choice keeps a job running, and each one turns a data problem into a wrong total that nobody sees.

Spark 4.0 switched ANSI mode on by default (spark.sql.ansi.enabled = true). The name comes from ANSI, the American standards body behind the SQL standard, and Spark then follows the standard's rules. An invalid conversion, an overflow (a number too big for its type) or a division by zero raises an error that names the problem, such as CAST_INVALID_INPUT or ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW. The error also carries a standard code, its SQLSTATE, and the job stops. The Try it runs the same expressions both ways:

Expression ANSI off (Spark 3) ANSI on (Spark 4)
CAST('12,50' AS INT) NULL CAST_INVALID_INPUT
CAST(25000000 AS INT) * 100 -1794967296 ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW
1250 / 0 NULL DIVIDE_BY_ZERO
CAST(300 AS TINYINT) 44 CAST_OVERFLOW

The second row is the dangerous one. 25 million euros in cents is 2.5 billion, which doesn't fit an INT, and Spark 3 answered with a negative number that looks like a refund. (The last row is a TINYINT, which holds only -128 to 127.)

Stopping is the right default, but a nightly job can't stop for good over one bad line either. So for each column, you decide what a bad value means, and you say it in code. Where a bad value should become NULL, use the try_ functions: try_cast, try_add, try_subtract, try_multiply, try_divide, and try_sum and try_avg for totals and averages. Each returns NULL exactly where the plain version would have raised the error, so you can count those rows and send them to a person. Where the value is right and the type is too small, use a wider type. A BIGINT is a 64-bit whole number, so CAST(25000000 AS BIGINT) * 100 is 2,500,000,000.

The errors beat the old NULLs for a second reason: they have a name your code can check. A Kotlin job can catch SparkThrowable and read getCondition(), and the lab's tests do exactly that.

A blank that hides a bad value is a wrong answer. Decide what a bad value means, and write it down. When an upgrade makes an old job fail, the error is almost always pointing at data that was already wrong.

Bad numbers are one kind of messy data. Next comes a messier kind: documents whose shape keeps changing.

try.title: The same expressions with ANSI off and on
steps: From the labs folder, run AnsiDemo. For six expressions, it prints the result with spark.sql.ansi.enabled off and on, then the try_ versions.
Before you read: which of the six do you expect to give a number with ANSI off? Which number?

code.title: AnsiDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l09.demo /** * The same expressions with ANSI mode off (Spark 3's default) and on (Spark 4's default), then the * try_ functions that give null on purpose. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() println("spark.sql.ansi.enabled by default: ${spark.conf().get("spark.sql.ansi.enabled")}") val cases = listOf( "CAST('12,50' AS INT)" to "a decimal comma in a settlement file", "CAST('2026-13-01' AS DATE)" to "month 13", "CAST(25000000 AS INT) * 100" to "25 million euros in cents, as INT", "CAST(300 AS TINYINT)" to "a value too big for the type", "1250 / 0" to "an fx rate of zero", "element_at(array(10, 20, 30), 5)" to "the 5th of 3 elements", ) for ((sql, what) in cases) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "false") val off = valueOrError(spark, "SELECT $sql") spark.conf().set("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "true") val on = valueOrError(spark, "SELECT $sql") println("%-34s (%s)\n ANSI off: %s\n ANSI on: %s".format(sql, what, off, on)) } println("the safe versions, ANSI on:") for (sql in listOf("try_cast('12,50' AS INT)", "try_multiply(CAST(25000000 AS INT), 100)", "try_divide(1250, 0)", "try_element_at(array(10, 20, 30), 5)", "CAST(25000000 AS BIGINT) * 100")) { println(" %-42s -> %s".format(sql, valueOrError(spark, "SELECT $sql"))) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
spark.sql.ansi.enabled by default: true
CAST('12,50' AS INT)               (a decimal comma in a settlement file)
    ANSI off: NULL
    ANSI on:  SparkNumberFormatException: [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value '12,50' of the type "STRING" cannot be cast to "INT" because it is malformed
CAST('2026-13-01' AS DATE)         (month 13)
    ANSI off: NULL
    ANSI on:  SparkDateTimeException: [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value '2026-13-01' of the type "STRING" cannot be cast to "DATE" because it is malfor
CAST(25000000 AS INT) * 100        (25 million euros in cents, as INT)
    ANSI off: -1794967296
    ANSI on:  SparkArithmeticException: [ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW] integer overflow
CAST(300 AS TINYINT)               (a value too big for the type)
    ANSI off: 44
    ANSI on:  SparkArithmeticException: [CAST_OVERFLOW] The value 300 of the type "INT" cannot be cast to "TINYINT" due to an overflow
1250 / 0                           (an fx rate of zero)
    ANSI off: NULL
    ANSI on:  SparkArithmeticException: [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] Division by zero
element_at(array(10, 20, 30), 5)   (the 5th of 3 elements)
    ANSI off: NULL
    ANSI on:  SparkArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: [INVALID_ARRAY_INDEX_IN_ELEMENT_AT] The index 5 is out of bounds
the safe versions, ANSI on:
    try_cast('12,50' AS INT)                   -> NULL
    try_multiply(CAST(25000000 AS INT), 100)   -> NULL
    try_divide(1250, 0)                        -> NULL
    try_element_at(array(10, 20, 30), 5)       -> NULL
    CAST(25000000 AS BIGINT) * 100             -> 2500000000

With ANSI off, four of the six expressions quietly returned NULL and two returned wrong numbers: 25 million euros in cents wrapped around to -1,794,967,296, and 300 became 44 (300 minus 256). With ANSI on, every one of them stopped with a named error. The try_ versions return NULL on purpose, and a wider type removes the overflow: as a BIGINT the amount is 2,500,000,000. The error messages are cut after their first sentence; the full text also says which try_ function to use and gives the SQLSTATE.

sections.h: Storing JSON whose shape keeps changing: VARIANT
sections.html:
Another company checks each card payment for signs of fraud and sends back a short message about it: a risk score, the card's country, the rules that fired. A message that one company's program pushes to another's like this is called a webhook. It's written in JSON, a common text format for structured data: names and values inside curly braces, which can nest. Here's one, 126 bytes long:

{"type":"authorization","amount":1250,"card":{"country":"NL","bin":"411111"},"risk":{"score":0.93,"rules":["velocity","geo"]}}

The shape keeps changing: a new rules list this month, an amount that became a nested object last quarter. How do you store that in a table?

Version 1: as a STRING column (text), and read it in every query with get_json_object(body, '$.card.country'). The $.card.country part is a path: start at the top, go into card, take country. Nothing is lost, and nothing breaks when a field appears. But every query reads and takes apart the whole text of every row again, once per field it asks for. And the column has no types: a score is only characters.

Version 2: take the text apart once, into a fixed STRUCT (a column with named, typed parts), with from_json(body, schema). Reads are fast and typed. But the schema, the list of fields and their types, is a guess about the future. A new field is silently dropped, and a field that changes type becomes NULL.

Version 3: VARIANT, a data type added in Spark 4.0. parse_json(body) reads the text once and stores the result as two byte arrays. The metadata is a dictionary of the field names used in the document. The value is a tree of typed values in binary. An object stores its field numbers sorted by name, with offsets (positions), so finding card is a binary search, not a walk through text. (A binary search opens a sorted list in the middle and keeps halving.) Numbers are stored as numbers. Every field is kept, whatever its shape, and a number like 0.93 is stored as an exact decimal. In the Try it, the webhook above becomes 49 bytes of field names and 76 bytes of typed values. That's no smaller for one document, but nothing in it ever needs reading from text again.

You read a variant with a path and the type you want:

SELECT variant_get(event, '$.card.country', 'string') AS country,   -- or the short form:
       event:risk.score::double                       AS score
FROM events

variant_get fails with INVALID_VARIANT_CAST when a value can't be turned into the type you asked for. try_variant_get returns NULL instead, and it will turn the string "0.85" into the number 0.85. schema_of_variant tells you what a document holds, which is how you'd discover that the fraud checker started sending amounts as objects.

Spark 4.1 made two improvements generally available. VARIANT is on by default, and shredding can store frequent fields as ordinary typed columns in the Parquet file (the column-by-column file format from lesson 5), next to the binary rest. A filter on one field then reads one narrow column. Spark 4.3 added functions that change a variant value in place, such as variant_set and variant_insert. In the Try it, 300,000 events stored as VARIANT took 3.3 MB of Parquet against 8.1 MB as text. The same count of high-risk events took about 40% less time on the variant column, with the same answer.

VARIANT, ANSI mode and Connect all live inside Spark. The last choice is yours: how you write the query in Kotlin.

try.title: Ask the same question of JSON text and of VARIANT
steps: From the labs folder, run VariantDemo. It reads one webhook into a VARIANT and takes fields out of it. Then it writes 300,000 events twice, as JSON text and as VARIANT, and runs the same high-risk count on both.
Look at the to_json line, which turns a variant back into text. Why did the names come back in a different order?
Compare the two times and the two sizes on disk.

code.title: VariantDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l09.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.SaveMode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.concat import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.element_at import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.array import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.hash import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.pmod import org.apache.spark.unsafe.types.VariantVal import java.io.File /** * Webhook events as JSON text and as VARIANT: what one variant holds, how fields come out of it, * and the same question asked of 300,000 events stored both ways in Parquet. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val body = """{"type":"authorization","amount":1250,"card":{"country":"NL","bin":"411111"},"risk":{"score":0.93,"rules":["velocity","geo"]}}""" val one = spark.sql("SELECT parse_json('$body') AS event") val v = one.first().get(0) as VariantVal println("JSON text: ${body.length} bytes; the variant: ${v.metadata.size} bytes of field names + ${v.value.size} bytes of values") println("schema_of_variant: " + one.selectExpr("schema_of_variant(event)").first().getString(0)) println("event:card.country::string -> " + one.selectExpr("event:card.country::string").first().getString(0)) println("variant_get(event, '$.risk.score', 'double') -> " + one.selectExpr("variant_get(event, '$.risk.score', 'double')").first().get(0)) println("to_json(parse_json('{\"b\":1,\"a\":2}')) -> " + spark.sql("SELECT to_json(parse_json('{\"b\":1,\"a\":2}'))").first().getString(0)) // 300,000 events: write them once as text and once as variant val text = File("build/l08/events-text") val variant = File("build/l08/events-variant") if (!File(variant, "_SUCCESS").exists()) { val events = spark.range(0, 300_000, 1, 4).select( col("id").alias("event_id"), concat( lit("""{"type":"authorization","amount":"""), pmod(hash(col("id")), lit(250_000)).cast("string"), lit(""","card":{"country":""""), element_at(array(lit("NL"), lit("DE"), lit("FR"), lit("GB")), pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(1)), lit(4)).plus(1)), lit(""""},"risk":{"score":"""), pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(2)), lit(100)).divide(100).cast("string"), lit(""","rules":["velocity"]},"merchant":{"id":"""), pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(3)), lit(500)).cast("string"), lit(""","name":"Merchant shop"}}"""), ).alias("body"), ) events.write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).parquet(text.absolutePath) spark.read().parquet(text.absolutePath).selectExpr("event_id", "parse_json(body) AS event") .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).parquet(variant.absolutePath) } fun size(dir: File) = dir.listFiles { f -> f.name.endsWith(".parquet") }!!.sumOf { it.length() } println("on disk: text %,d bytes, variant %,d bytes".format(size(text), size(variant))) spark.read().parquet(text.absolutePath).createOrReplaceTempView("events_text") spark.read().parquet(variant.absolutePath).createOrReplaceTempView("events_variant") val asText = """SELECT get_json_object(body, '$.card.country') AS country, count(*) AS high_risk FROM events_text WHERE CAST(get_json_object(body, '$.risk.score') AS DOUBLE) > 0.8 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""" val asVariant = """SELECT event:card.country::string AS country, count(*) AS high_risk FROM events_variant WHERE event:risk.score::double > 0.8 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""" for ((label, sql) in listOf("text, parsed by every query" to asText, "variant, parsed once" to asVariant)) { spark.sql(sql).collectAsList() // warm-up val t0 = System.nanoTime() val rows = (1..3).map { spark.sql(sql).collectAsList() }.last() println("%-28s average of 3: %5.0f ms %s".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 3e6, rows)) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
JSON text: 126 bytes; the variant: 49 bytes of field names + 76 bytes of values
schema_of_variant: OBJECT<amount: BIGINT, card: OBJECT<bin: STRING, country: STRING>, risk: OBJECT<rules: ARRAY<STRING>, score: DECIMAL(2,2)>, type: STRING>
event:card.country::string -> NL
variant_get(event, '$.risk.score', 'double') -> 0.93
to_json(parse_json('{"b":1,"a":2}')) -> {"a":2,"b":1}
on disk: text 8,086,693 bytes, variant 3,343,970 bytes
text, parsed by every query  average of 3:  6951 ms  [[DE,14297], [FR,14220], [GB,14230], [NL,14044]]
variant, parsed once         average of 3:  4101 ms  [[DE,14297], [FR,14220], [GB,14230], [NL,14044]]

schema_of_variant shows the types the variant kept: the amount is a BIGINT, the score an exact DECIMAL(2,2) (two digits, both after the point), and the fields come out sorted by name. That's the order to_json printed {"a":2,"b":1} in, because it's how a variant object stores its fields, so that a lookup can search them by name. Both queries give the same counts. The text query takes every JSON document apart again, twice per row (once per field it reads), on every run; the variant query reads the binary values directly. Times depend on your computer, so look at the ratio between the two lines.

sections.h: Writing Spark queries in Kotlin that the optimizer can read
sections.html:
You write Spark from Kotlin through Spark's Java API, the set of calls Spark offers to Java programs, because Kotlin can call Java code directly. JetBrains, the company that makes Kotlin, once had a Kotlin wrapper for Spark, kotlin-spark-api. It stops at Spark 3.3.2, and its README (the project's front page) says Spark 4 support proved "near impossible" with its design. That leaves three ways to say what you want, and they're not equal.

The first two are column expressions and SQL. An expression is a small formula over columns, such as "status equals CAPTURED" (a captured payment is one whose money has really moved). where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")), spark.sql("SELECT ...") and SQL pipe syntax all produce the same thing: a tree of expressions that Catalyst, Spark's optimizer, can read. Pipe syntax, new in Spark 4.0, writes a query in the order the data flows, one step per line after |>:

FROM payments
|> WHERE status = 'CAPTURED'
|> AGGREGATE sum(amount_cents) AS total GROUP BY merchant_id

That reads like a chain of Kotlin calls, and it's only a different spelling. The Try it shows that classic SQL, pipe SQL and the DataFrame API give the same optimized plan, and all three hand status = 'CAPTURED' to the Parquet reader.

The third way is a typed Dataset, a table whose rows are objects of a class you write, tested with lambdas. spark.table("payments").as(Encoders.bean(PaymentBean::class.java)).filter { it.status == "CAPTURED" } feels the most like Kotlin: each row becomes an object, and a lambda tests it. Two things cost you. The encoder, the part that turns rows into objects, needs a Java bean. That's a class with a no-argument constructor and a getter and setter per column, which a Kotlin data class with vals is not. And the lambda is compiled JVM code that Catalyst can call but can't read. It can't move it, simplify it or hand it to the file reader. In the Try it, the lambda version's file scan is handed no filter at all (PushedFilters: []), so it reads every row. Its plan has a Filter that builds a PaymentBean from every row (initializejavabean) only to call your lambda on it. With Spark Connect, the lambda also needs its class uploaded to the server (first section).

Think of the restaurant again. "No onions" is an instruction the kitchen can read, so it plans around it before cooking. A sealed envelope marked "do this to each plate" can only be opened plate by plate, after the cooking.

Say what you want in expressions Spark can read. Keep lambdas for logic that has no expression. When you must call your own code for each row, a user-defined function (UDF), registered once under a name, is clearer than a lambda in a chain. It's as closed to the optimizer as a lambda, though.

try.title: One question, four spellings
steps: From the labs folder, run KotlinApiDemo. It asks for captured totals per shop in classic SQL, pipe SQL, the DataFrame API and a typed Dataset with a Kotlin lambda. For each, it prints whether the optimized plan matches classic SQL's and what the Parquet scan was asked to filter.
Predict which spellings hand the status filter to the scan.
Look at the trimmed plan of the lambda version. Where is your Kotlin code in it?

code.title: KotlinApiDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l09.demo import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.FilterFunction import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum /** A Java bean, so Encoders.bean can map rows to it: a no-argument constructor and a getter and setter per column. */ class PaymentBean { var payment_id: Long = 0 var merchant_id: Int = 0 var status: String = "" var amount_cents: Long = 0 } /** * One question asked four ways from Kotlin: classic SQL, SQL pipe syntax, the DataFrame API and a * typed Dataset with a Kotlin lambda. Prints whether the plans match and what the file scan was * asked to filter. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() demoPayments(spark).createOrReplaceTempView("payments") val classic = spark.sql( """ SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM payments WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' GROUP BY merchant_id """.trimIndent() ) val pipe = spark.sql( """ FROM payments |> WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' |> AGGREGATE sum(amount_cents) AS total GROUP BY merchant_id """.trimIndent() ) val frame = spark.table("payments").where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")) .groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total")) val typed = spark.table("payments").`as`(Encoders.bean(PaymentBean::class.java)) .filter(FilterFunction { it.status == "CAPTURED" }) // Kotlin code: Spark can only call it .toDF().groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total")) val reference = classic.queryExecution().optimizedPlan() for ((label, df) in listOf("classic SQL" to classic, "pipe SQL" to pipe, "DataFrame API" to frame, "typed lambda" to typed)) { val same = df.queryExecution().optimizedPlan().sameResult(reference) val scan = df.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString().lines().first { "FileScan" in it } val pushed = Regex("""PushedFilters: \[([^\]]*)]""").find(scan)!!.groupValues[1] val first = df.orderBy("merchant_id").first() println("%-14s same plan as classic SQL: %-5s pushed to Parquet: [%s] merchant %d total %,d".format( label, same, pushed, first.getInt(0), first.getLong(1))) } println("typed lambda plan, trimmed:") typed.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString().lines() .filter { "Filter" in it || "DeserializeToObject" in it || "SerializeFromObject" in it } .forEach { println(" " + it.trim().replace(Regex("#\\d+L?"), "").take(110)) } spark.stop() }

try.expect:
classic SQL    same plan as classic SQL: true   pushed to Parquet: [IsNotNull(status), EqualTo(status,CAPTURED)]  merchant 0 total 24,095,043
pipe SQL       same plan as classic SQL: true   pushed to Parquet: [IsNotNull(status), EqualTo(status,CAPTURED)]  merchant 0 total 24,095,043
DataFrame API  same plan as classic SQL: true   pushed to Parquet: [IsNotNull(status), EqualTo(status,CAPTURED)]  merchant 0 total 24,095,043
typed lambda   same plan as classic SQL: false  pushed to Parquet: []  merchant 0 total 24,095,043
typed lambda plan, trimmed:
  +- Filter invoke(sfz.batch.l09.demo.KotlinApiDemoKt$$Lambda/0x0000008000f847e0@57421e4e.call(initializejavab
  +- FileScan parquet [payment_id,merchant_id,status,amount_cents] Batched: true, DataFilters: [], Format: Parqu

Classic SQL, pipe SQL and the DataFrame API produce plans that sameResult calls equal, and all three hand status = 'CAPTURED' to the Parquet reader. The typed lambda gives the same totals by a longer route. Its scan reads every row of four columns with nothing pushed, and the Filter above it calls KotlinApiDemoKt$$Lambda...call(initializejavabean(...)): it builds an object per row and calls into your code. The lambda's name and address change from run to run. The plan lines are cut at 110 characters.

opening:
Picture a café owner adding up a day's card payments in a spreadsheet. One line says 12,50, because someone typed the amount with a comma, the way much of Europe writes it. The spreadsheet can't read that as a number, so it leaves the cell out of the sum without a word. The total is 12.50 short, and it looks perfectly normal.

A program that keeps going feels better than one that stops. Spark 3 made that choice for years: a value it couldn't read became a blank, and the job carried on. But a total that's quietly wrong is worse than an error, because nobody goes looking for it.

In The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching, we watched Spark plan and correct a query inside one program. In this lesson, we'll see what Spark 4 changed for anyone who calls it from their own Java or Kotlin code. We'll meet a client that sends plans to a Spark server, errors in place of silent blanks, a type for JSON (a common text format for data), and Kotlin the optimizer can read. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a spreadsheet that left 12,50 out of a total without a word. Spark 3 did the same. Spark 4 stops with CAST_INVALID_INPUT instead, so the choice of what a bad value means is back in your code, where try_cast makes it visible.

Open a spreadsheet, type a few amounts into a column with one of them written as 12,50, and add the column up. See whether it complains or quietly leaves the cell out. (With some language settings, it reads 12,50 as a number.)

Next, we'll turn from the engine to the tables it reads, and ask how to shape payment data so that questions about years of history stay simple and fast.

compare.title: The same payout total: Spark 3's defaults and Spark 4's

a.label: Spark 3: ANSI off
a.title: Spark 3: ANSI off
a.html:
SELECT CAST('12,50' AS INT)            -> NULL
SELECT CAST(25000000 AS INT) * 100     -> -1794967296
SELECT 1250 / 0                        -> NULL

sum over the file: wrong, and the job is green

b.label: Spark 4: ANSI on
b.title: Spark 4: ANSI on
b.html:
SELECT CAST('12,50' AS INT)            -> [CAST_INVALID_INPUT]
SELECT CAST(25000000 AS INT) * 100     -> [ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW]
SELECT 1250 / 0                        -> [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO]

try_cast / try_multiply / try_divide -> NULL, on purpose

compare.note: Both columns come from AnsiDemo. Spark 3's defaults never stop a job: each bad value becomes a NULL or a wrapped number, and the damage shows up later as a total that doesn't add up. Spark 4's defaults stop at the first bad value with a named error, which turns a hidden data problem into a visible one. The try_ functions are the bridge between them. They bring back the NULL, but only where you wrote them, so the choice sits in the code where a reviewer can see it.

worked.title: Move a nightly payout job to Spark 4

steps.say: After the upgrade to Spark 4.1, the nightly job that reads the payout file fails. The error names the problem and the function to use. Read it before you touch any setting.
steps.code:
org.apache.spark.SparkNumberFormatException: [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value '12,50' of the type "STRING"
  cannot be cast to "BIGINT" because it is malformed. ... Use `try_cast` to tolerate malformed input
  and return NULL instead. SQLSTATE: 22018

steps.say: Find out how many lines are affected and what they look like. ANSI mode has told you something Spark 3 hid: some lines were silently NULL for years. (The file names and counts here are made up for teaching.)
steps.code: // 1. how bad is it? lines.where(col("amount_text").try_cast("bigint").isNull()).groupBy("source_file").count().show() // source_file count // visa-2026-11-06.csv 14 <- decimal commas from one card company

steps.say: Decide per column. A malformed amount means a rejected line: convert it with try_cast and send the NULLs to a table of rejects. An overflow means the type is too small for the arithmetic, so widen it rather than hide it. Here the amount is multiplied by an exchange rate stored in millionths (rate_ppm), so the product goes into a DECIMAL(38,0), a number with room for 38 digits.
steps.code: // 2. say what a bad value means, in code val parsed = lines .withColumn("amount_minor", col("amount_text").try_cast("bigint")) .withColumn("eur_ppm", col("amount_minor").cast("decimal(38,0)").multiply(col("rate_ppm"))) // 38 digits: room for any real amount parsed.where(col("amount_minor").isNull()).writeTo("settlement.rejects").append()

steps.say: Keep the rest of Spark 4's defaults, and check the totals against last month's run on Spark 3. Any difference is a row Spark 3 was getting wrong.
steps.code:
// 3. compare: the Spark 3 total skipped the null lines; the new total plus the rejects should explain the gap
// never: spark.conf().set("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "false")

lab.title: Make a payout-file parser ANSI-safe and read webhooks as VARIANT
steps: Run the tests. AnsiTest fails because SettlementLines.parse is the Spark 3 code: under Spark 4's ANSI mode, the line '12,50' stops the whole job with CAST_INVALID_INPUT. VariantTest fails on TODOs.
Fix parse so that every line survives: a bad amount and a product that overflows both become NULL. Then write rejects, which keeps the lines that parse couldn't convert, so a person can look at them.
Write WebhookEvents.parse: one VARIANT column, event, read once from the JSON text. A broken body gives a NULL event, not a failed job.
Write highRiskByCountry. The score is sometimes a number and sometimes the string "0.85", and capture events (sent when the money moves) have no score at all.
Write amountMinor. Old events send "amount": 1250, and new ones send "amount": {"value": "12.50", ...}. Both must come out as 1250, the amount in cents.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Column.try_cast("bigint") and functions.try_multiply(a, b) give NULL where cast and multiply would throw an error.

try_parse_json(col("body")) makes the VARIANT. variant_get(col("event"), "$.card.country", "string") reads a field; try_variant_get returns NULL when the value is missing or can't be converted, and it turns the string "0.85" into 0.85 for you.

For the amount, use coalesce( the old shape as bigint, the new shape's $.amount.value as decimal(12,2) times 100 cast to bigint ). coalesce returns its first argument that isn't NULL. Reading an object as bigint with try_variant_get gives NULL, so the coalesce falls through to the second.
lab.done: All seven tests in AnsiTest and VariantTest pass.

drill.title: Three Spark 4 one-liners
drill.prompt: From memory, in Kotlin: (1) connect to a Spark Connect server on this computer's default port; (2) turn a text column amount_text into a BIGINT so that bad values become NULL under ANSI mode; (3) read the nested field card.country as a string from a VARIANT column event. Then say which of the three lines sends anything to the server.

answer.html: // 1. a thin client: no master, no executors in this JVM val spark = SparkSession.builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate() // 2. ANSI-safe cast: null instead of CAST_INVALID_INPUT val amounts = lines.withColumn("amount_minor", col("amount_text").try_cast("bigint")) // 3. one field out of a VARIANT, no JSON text parsed val countries = events.select(variant_get(col("event"), "$.card.country", "string")) // only line 1 talks to the server (it opens the session). Lines 2 and 3 add nodes to a plan in this JVM; // nothing is sent until an action, and with Connect that is also when a misspelled column name fails

recap: Spark Connect splits your program from Spark: the client sends an unchecked plan as protobuf over gRPC (port 15002), and the server checks it, optimizes it, runs it and streams Arrow batches back.
A Connect client has no SparkContext and no RDDs, and a lambda runs only after its class files are uploaded with registerClassFinder or addArtifact.

Spark 4.0 turned ANSI mode on: bad conversions, overflows and division by zero stop the job with a named error, where Spark 3 gave a NULL or a wrapped number. try_cast, try_add, try_multiply and try_divide give NULL on purpose.
VARIANT stores JSON read once, as a dictionary of field names plus typed binary values; variant_get and : paths read fields without reading the text again.
From Kotlin, use the Java API with column expressions or SQL (pipe syntax is only a spelling). Typed lambdas are closed to Catalyst, so no filter is pushed through them.

The limits: Connect can't carry anything that lives only in a driver, ANSI mode only finds bad values (you still decide what they mean), and VARIANT saves nothing on one document. It pays off when many queries read the same fields.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a Spark Connect client can't call rdd() but can run df.groupBy("merchant_id").count(), and what it would take to run a Kotlin lambda through Connect.
explain.answer: A Connect client never runs Spark itself. A DataFrame in the client is only a tree of plan steps built from column expressions: read these files, filter on this column, group by that one. On an action, the client encodes the tree as protobuf and sends it over gRPC to the server. There the driver checks the names, optimizes the plan, runs it on its executors and streams the result back as Arrow batches. groupBy(...).count() is just more plan steps, so it travels fine. An RDD is different. It's a handle on data spread over the cluster inside a running SparkContext, with partitions and lineage held in the driver's memory, and its operations are your JVM functions applied to objects. None of that exists in the client's process, so rdd() and sparkContext() throw. A lambda is the same problem in small: the plan can name it, but its compiled code lives in your client's classes, not on the server. To run it, the client must upload those class files first, with registerClassFinder for a classes folder or addArtifact for a jar, and then the server can load the class and call it. Even then Catalyst can't see inside it, so prefer column expressions.

deeper.html:
Connect comes with a few more pieces. Spark 4.1 added a JDBC driver for Spark Connect. JDBC is Java's standard way for programs to talk to databases, so a tool that only speaks JDBC can send SQL to a Connect server; Spark 4.3 taught that driver complex types and SQLSTATE error codes. The Python side can run without any JVM at all: the pyspark-client package is pure Python. Sessions on a Connect server are kept apart, each with its own temporary views and settings, which is what lets one server answer many programs.

VARIANT has a storage trick worth knowing for big tables: shredding. When most events share some fields, the writer can store those fields as ordinary typed Parquet columns next to the variant's binary rest. A query on event:card.country then reads one narrow column with min and max statistics (lesson 5) instead of every variant value. Spark 4.1 made shredding generally available, and Iceberg's format version 3 (lesson 11) defines the same VARIANT type, so other engines can read it.

SQL pipe syntax keeps growing. Spark 4.2 allowed aggregates inside |> SELECT and accepts | as a shorter spelling of |>. ANSI mode also has a second half that this lesson skipped: type coercion, the rules for mixing types in one expression. With ANSI on, Spark follows the standard's rules, so 'abc' = 1 tries to turn 'abc' into a number and fails, where Spark 3 returned NULL. spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy, ANSI by default, applies the same strictness when an INSERT puts a value into a column of a narrower type.

Spark 4.3 also added SQL that later lessons of this track use: an ASOF JOIN (off by default), which lesson 14 uses for point-in-time joins, and type 2 dimension flows in Declarative Pipelines, which lesson 10 builds by hand. When Iceberg and Delta ship builds for Spark 4.3, moving the labs up is a one-line change in labs/bigdata/build.gradle.kts.
